event:越南国成立.note: On 8 March Bảo Đại and French President Auriol signed the Élysée Accords; Cochinchina was incorporated in June, and on 1 July the French-backed State of Vietnam was established, with Bảo Đại as head of state.

event:越南国独立条约.note: French Prime Minister Laniel and Nguyễn Phúc Bửu Lộc, Prime Minister of the State of Vietnam, initialled the Treaty of Independence and the Treaty of Association in Paris, by which France recognized Vietnam's full independence. Bảo Đại then appointed Ngô Đình Diệm prime minister, who formed his cabinet on 7 July.
event:越南国独立条约.old: Treaty of Independence of the State of Vietnam

event:越南民主共和国成立.mod: Ba Đình Square, Hà Nội, Vietnam
event:越南民主共和国成立.note: Hồ Chí Minh read the Declaration of Independence in Ba Đình Square, quoting the US Declaration of Independence and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man. The same month Chinese troops entered northern Vietnam to accept the surrender and British troops entered southern Vietnam; the French colonial army soon reoccupied Sài Gòn.

event:达德拉与纳加尔哈维利脱离葡萄牙.note: Volunteers from the United Front of Goans and other groups favouring merger with India seized the Portuguese inland enclaves of Dadra (22 July) and Silvassa, the chief town of Nagar Haveli (2 August), and set up a self-governing administration; the territory was incorporated into India in 1961. Portugal later took the case to the International Court of Justice.
event:达德拉与纳加尔哈维利脱离葡萄牙.old: Dadra and Nagar Haveli break away from Portugal

event:达林条约.note: Ibn Saud signed a treaty with Cox, the British Political Resident in the Gulf: Britain recognized his rule over Nejd and Hasa and took them under its protection; Ibn Saud undertook not to conclude treaties with other powers and not to attack the Gulf sheikhdoms under British protection.

event:达赖亲政与出走亚东.note: After the Qamdo Campaign the 14th Dalai Lama assumed power ahead of time; the Kashag's “appeal” to the United Nations was not placed on the agenda. In December the Dalai Lama left Lhasa for Yadong to wait and see.
event:达赖亲政与出走亚东.old: Dalai Lama assumes power and leaves for Yadong

event:达赖喇嘛返回拉萨.note: The 14th Dalai Lama returned from Yadong to Lhasa; in September the Local Government of Xizang held a meeting to discuss the agreement, and on 24 October the Dalai Lama telegraphed Mao Zedong to express his support for it.

event:达赖喇嘛返拉萨.note: After the expulsion of the Sichuan Army, the 13th Dalai Lama returned from India via Yadong to Lhasa and in February issued a proclamation that he would manage political and religious affairs on his own; the same year he privately concluded the so-called Mongolia–Xizang Treaty with Outer Mongolia, a treaty the Chinese government did not recognize.

event:远东共和国并入苏俄.note: The People's Assembly of the Far Eastern Republic voted to dissolve itself and merge into the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic; on 30 December the Soviet Union was founded.
event:远东共和国并入苏俄.old: Far Eastern Republic merged into Soviet Russia

event:远东共和国成立.note: The Congress of the Working People of the Baikal Region in Verkhneudinsk proclaimed the Far Eastern Republic, which Soviet Russia recognized in May. Its democratic-republic façade avoided a direct clash with Japan, but it was in fact controlled by the Far Eastern Bureau of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks).

event:远东建设总局设立.note: The Soviet Union set up Dalstroy, using Gulag prisoners to mine gold in Kolyma; Magadan grew up as a result, and “Kolyma” became a byword for the labour camps.

event:远东朝鲜人强制迁徙.note: On the pretext of guarding against Japanese espionage, the Soviet Union forcibly deported the entire Korean population of the Far East, about 170,000 people, to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan; many died on the way and in the early period of resettlement.
event:远东朝鲜人强制迁徙.old: Deportation of Koreans from the Soviet Far East

event:退出印度运动.note: At its Bombay meeting the Indian National Congress passed the “Quit India” resolution, and Gandhi called on the people to “Do or Die”. The next day Gandhi, Nehru and all the other leaders were arrested by the British colonial authorities; crowds everywhere sabotaged railways and telegraph lines and were suppressed, and more than 100,000 people were jailed.

event:通道会议.note: After the Battle of the Xiang River, the central leaders held an ad hoc consultation at Tongdao and adopted Mao Zedong's proposal to give up going north to western Hunan to join the Red Second and Sixth Army Groups and to turn instead towards Guizhou, where KMT forces were weak.

event:遵义会议.note: An enlarged meeting of the Political Bureau held at Bai Huizhang's residence in Zunyi concentrated on correcting the military errors of Bo Gu and Otto Braun and elected Mao Zedong to the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau; a three-man military group of Zhou Enlai, Mao Zedong and Wang Jiaxiang was then formed. The meeting in effect established Mao Zedong's leading position in the Party Central Committee and the Red Army, and was a turning point of life-and-death significance in the history of the Party.

event:鄂木斯克政变.note: Cossack officers arrested the Socialist Revolutionaries in the Ufa Directory, and the Council of Ministers named Admiral Kolchak “Supreme Ruler of Russia”; the Siberian Whites were nominally brought under one command.

event:重庆谈判.note: Responding to Chiang Kai-shek's three telegraphed invitations, Mao Zedong flew to Chongqing accompanied by US Ambassador Hurley. In forty-three days of negotiations the two sides set the basic policy of peaceful national reconstruction and agreed to convene a Political Consultative Conference, but reached no agreement on the questions of the armed forces and the governments of the Liberated Areas.

event:金圆券改革.note: The KMT government abolished the fabi and issued gold yuan notes, compulsorily buying in gold, silver and foreign exchange and imposing price controls, with Chiang Ching-kuo supervising in Shanghai. The price controls collapsed after little more than two months; prices soared, the economy of the KMT-controlled areas teetered on the brink of collapse, and the government lost all popular support.

event:锡兰独立.note: Ceylon peacefully became a dominion within the Commonwealth, with Senanayake as its first prime minister; Britain kept the naval base at Trincomalee and the air base at Katunayake.

event:锦州轰炸.note: After the Liaoning provincial government and the Headquarters of the Northeastern Frontier Defence Army moved to Jinzhou, aircraft of the Japanese Kwantung Army bombed the city—the first air raid on a city since the First World War—drawing the attention of the League of Nations.

event:镇压反革命运动.note: The CPC Central Committee issued the Directive on Correcting the Rightist Deviation in Suppressing Counter-revolutionary Activities (the Double Ten Directive), and a large-scale campaign to suppress counter-revolutionaries was then launched nationwide.

event:长崎原子弹.note: US forces dropped the plutonium bomb “Fat Man” on Nagasaki; by the end of the year about 74,000 people had died. The same day the Soviet Red Army launched its offensive into Northeast China; that night, at an imperial conference, the emperor decided to accept the Potsdam Proclamation on condition that the emperor's position be preserved.

event:阿卜杜拉国王遇刺.note: King Abdullah I of Jordan was shot dead by a young Palestinian while attending Friday prayers at the Al-Aqsa Mosque in the Old City of Jerusalem, with his grandson Hussein at his side. His eldest son Talal succeeded him but was deposed on grounds of illness in August of the following year, and Hussein came to the throne.

event:阿塔图尔克逝世.note: Kemal Atatürk died of illness at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, and İsmet İnönü succeeded him as president.

event:阿塞拜疆人民政府成立.note: Under Soviet occupation, Pishevari's Azerbaijan Democratic Party set up an autonomous government in Tabriz. The Soviet Union's delay in withdrawing its troops set off the Iran crisis, which the UN Security Council took up; Soviet troops left in May 1946, and in December the Iranian army marched in.

event:阿姆利则惨案.note: During the Punjab protests against the Rowlatt Act, the British Brigadier-General Dyer led troops to block the exits of Jallianwala Bagh and fired on the assembled crowd for about ten minutes; the official count was 379 dead, but the real toll was higher. The massacre pushed Gandhi towards all-out non-cooperation.

event:阿拉伯起义.note: Sharif Hussein rose in revolt in Mecca and declared his break with the Ottomans; Britain supplied gold and arms, and Lawrence and other officers accompanied the rebels. The rebel army advanced north along the Hejaz Railway and entered Damascus in 1918.

event:阿穆尔铁路贯通.note: The Amur River bridge at Khabarovsk was opened to traffic and the Amur Railway was completed along its whole length; from then on the Trans-Siberian Railway could run straight through to Vladivostok without crossing Northeast China.

event:陈宧宣布四川独立.note: Chen Yi, Yuan Shikai's confidant and General of Sichuan, announced that he had “severed personal relations” with Yuan and declared Sichuan independent, a particularly heavy blow to Yuan; on the 29th Tang Xiangming of Hunan followed suit.

event:陈炯明叛变.note: Sun Yat-sen insisted on the Northern Expedition and broke with Chen Jiongming. In the small hours of 16 June, Ye Ju and others of Chen Jiongming's forces rebelled and shelled the presidential residence on Guanyin Hill; Sun Yat-sen escaped aboard the warship Yongfeng and held out for more than fifty days before leaving for Shanghai on 9 August. Sun Yat-sen thus came to see that relying on warlords would not work, and turned to alliance with Soviet Russia.

event:陕甘宁边区政府成立.note: The former Northwest Office of the Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was renamed the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Government, nominally subordinate to the Nationalist Government, with its seat at Yan'an.

event:青岛归还.note: Under the Treaty for the Settlement of Outstanding Questions relative to Shandong, Japan returned Qingdao and the Jiaozhou Bay leased territory to China, and the Office of the Director-General of the Jiao'ao Commercial Port was set up; China redeemed the Qingdao–Jinan Railway, the Japanese garrison withdrew in stages, and the Shandong Question was settled for the time being.

event:韩复榘被处决.note: Han Fuju, chairman of the Shandong provincial government, abandoned Jinan and Tai'an without a fight; he was arrested at Kaifeng, taken to Wuchang and shot for disobeying orders, sending a shock through commanders everywhere.

event:食盐进军.note: Gandhi and 78 followers walked for 24 days, about 390 km, from the Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad to Dandi on the coast; on 6 April he made salt by boiling seawater in defiance of the salt-tax laws, setting off a nationwide civil disobedience movement in which more than 60,000 people were arrested.

event:香港秘密大营救.note: After the fall of Hong Kong, the CPC's Southern Work Committee and the Dongjiang guerrillas secretly escorted more than 800 cultural figures and democratic personages stranded in Hong Kong, among them He Xiangning, Liu Yazi, Mao Dun and Zou Taofen, through Kowloon and Bao'an to the interior, without losing a single one.

event:马占山再举抗日.note: Ma Zhanshan, who had for a time served as governor of Puppet Heilongjiang, slipped out of Qiqihar and at Heihe announced by circular telegram that he was returning to the national cause to resist Japan, rallying the volunteer armies of northern Northeast China; defeated at the end of the year, he withdrew into the Soviet Union.
event:马占山再举抗日.old: Ma Zhanshan resumes resistance to Japan

event:马哈巴德共和国.note: Qazi Muhammad proclaimed a Kurdish republic in Mahabad, with Barzani tribal forces as its main strength. It lasted less than a year before it was put down by the Iranian army.

event:马尼拉条约.note: Under US orchestration, the United States, Britain, France, Australia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Thailand and Pakistan signed the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty in Manila, forming the military bloc of the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization the following year; an attached protocol placed southern Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia under its protection. The United States had already concluded defence treaties with the Philippines (August 1951) and with Australia and New Zealand (September of the same year).

event:马日事变.note: Xu Kexiang, a National Revolutionary Army regimental commander stationed in Changsha, staged a counter-revolutionary mutiny, attacking the Hunan Provincial General Trade Union and the peasant associations and arresting and killing Communists and the worker and peasant masses; “countryside purges” followed across Hunan. The Wuhan Nationalist Government compromised and gave ground, and KMT–CPC relations deteriorated sharply.

event:马来亚“紧急状态”.note: Malayan Communist Party guerrillas shot dead three European plantation managers at Sungei Siput, Perak; the British colonial authorities declared an “Emergency” and banned the party. The Malayan Communist Party led the Malayan National Liberation Army into the jungle to wage armed struggle against British rule; from 1950 the British carried out the “Briggs Plan”, moving 500,000 Chinese into “New Villages”.

event:马来亚联合邦成立.note: In the face of Malay opposition, Britain abolished the Malayan Union and reorganized it as the Federation of Malaya, restoring the sovereignty of the sultans and strictly limiting the access of Chinese and Indians to citizenship.

event:马歇尔调处.note: US special envoy Marshall came to China to mediate the conflict between the KMT and the CPC, bringing about the ceasefire order of 10 January 1946 and the Executive Headquarters for Military Mediation in Beiping; in June the KMT launched a full-scale civil war and the fighting spread on all fronts; in January 1947 Marshall declared his mediation a failure and returned to the United States.

event:驼峰空运.note: After the Burma Road was cut, US forces and the China National Aviation Corporation flew from Assam in India over the southern flank of the Himalayas to Kunming, carrying in more than 600,000 tonnes of supplies in more than three years at the cost of several hundred aircraft. It was wartime China's main external supply line.

event:高尔察克被处决.note: To secure its safe passage east, the Czechoslovak Legion handed Kolchak over to the Political Centre in Irkutsk on 15 January; as remnants of the White army approached, the Bolshevik Revolutionary Committee had him executed on 7 February.

event:麦克阿瑟解职.note: MacArthur publicly advocated bombing Northeast China and using the KMT forces on Taiwan, in conflict with Truman's “limited war” policy, and was relieved of all his posts; Ridgway succeeded him as Commander-in-Chief of the “UN Command” and Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers in Japan.

event:黄埔军校开学.note: The Army Officers' Academy, founded through KMT–CPC cooperation, held its opening ceremony on Changzhou Island at Huangpu, Guangzhou, with Sun Yat-sen as director-general, Chiang Kai-shek as commandant and Liao Zhongkai as Party representative; the Soviet Union provided funds and weapons. The Whampoa student army became the backbone of the National Revolutionary Army.

event:黄花岗起义.note: Huang Xing led a Tongmenghui dare-to-die squad in an attack on the Liangguang viceroy's yamen; the attack failed, and the fallen were buried together at Huanghuagang (the 72 Martyrs). The Tongmenghui lost many of its core members, yet the revolution's momentum surged as a result.

event:黎巴嫩独立.note: The Lebanese parliament amended the constitution to remove the mandate provisions; on 11 November the Free French authorities arrested President Khoury, Prime Minister Solh and others, provoking nationwide protests and British pressure, and were forced to release them on the 22nd, which became Independence Day.

event:黎平会议.note: The Political Bureau formally decided to make the Sichuan–Guizhou border area the direction for a new base area, rejecting Otto Braun's insistence on still heading for western Hunan.

pass:乃堆拉山口.note: The pass on the trade route from Yadong to Sikkim and Kalimpong; in the later stages of the War of Resistance some aid supplies for China came from India through here into Xizang for onward transport.

pass:仙霞关.note: The pass in the Xianxia Mountains on the route between Zhejiang and Fujian; in the Battle of Zhejiang–Jiangxi of 1942 it was the screen of southwestern Zhejiang.

pass:佐吉拉山口.note: The only road pass from Srinagar to Ladakh, about 3,500 metres above sea level; in November 1948 Indian forces took the pass with tanks.

pass:冷口.note: A gateway in the Great Wall; Shang Zhen's forces lost it in April 1933, and the Japanese broke through here into the area east of the Luan River, forcing the Tanggu Truce.

pass:函谷关.note: The eastern entrance of the ancient Xiao–Han road and a key point on the Longhai Railway. In the Battle of Central Henan in 1944 the Japanese thrust west as far as the Lingbao line, where they were checked and pulled back.

pass:剑门关.note: The natural fortress on the Jinniu Road between Sichuan and Shaanxi. In April 1935, after forcing a crossing of the Jialing River, the Red Fourth Front Army took Jianmen Pass.

pass:南口.note: The southern end of the Guangou valley, where the Beijing–Suiyuan Railway enters the mountains. In 1926 the Guominjun fought the Zhili–Fengtian allied forces here for four months; in August 1937 Tang Enbo's forces held off the Japanese here for half a month.

pass:博兰山口.note: The pass from the plain of Sind to Quetta and Kandahar; the British built a railway through it, reaching Chaman on the Afghan border.

pass:古北口.note: The thoroughfare between Beijing and Rehe. In March–May 1933 the KMT Central Army's 17th Army fought a bloody battle here, the fiercest of the Great Wall Resistance.

pass:喜峰口.note: In the Great Wall Resistance of March 1933, the broadsword squads of Song Zheyuan's 29th Army raided the Japanese by night and won wide fame.

pass:嘉峪关.note: The western end of the Ming Great Wall and the way west out of the Hexi Corridor; the Northwest International Route passed through it on its way east.

pass:大散关.note: The northern entrance to the Qinling, where the Sichuan–Shaanxi Highway enters the mountains; during the War of Resistance it was the chokepoint of communications between Sichuan and the Northwest.

pass:夹金山.mod: Jiajin Mountain, on the Baoxing–Xiaojin border, Sichuan
pass:夹金山.note: A snowy pass more than 4,000 metres above sea level. In June 1935 the Central Red Army crossed it and joined the Red Fourth Front Army at Dawei, Maogong.

pass:娄山关.mod: Loushan Pass, on the Tongzi–Zunyi border, Guizhou
pass:娄山关.note: The key route between Sichuan and Guizhou. In February 1935, after the second crossing of the Chishui River, the Central Red Army took Loushan Pass and occupied Zunyi again.

pass:娘子关.note: The route by which the Zhengding–Taiyuan Railway enters Shanxi. Lost in the Battle of Niangzi Pass in October 1937; the Japanese advanced west along the Zhengding–Taiyuan Railway, and the gateway to Taiyuan lay wide open.

pass:居庸关.note: The key pass in the middle of the Guangou valley, through which the Beijing–Zhangjiakou Railway runs; it commands the northwestern gateway to Beijing.

pass:山海关.note: The eastern end of the Great Wall and the chokepoint between the lands inside and outside the Great Wall. Japanese forces took it in January 1933, after which the defence of Rehe and the Great Wall Resistance began; in November 1945 KMT forces attacked Shanhaiguan and the people's army rose to defend it, the prelude to the KMT forces' scramble to seize the Northeast.

pass:平型关.mod: Pingxing Pass, on the Fanshi–Lingqiu border, Shanxi
pass:平型关.note: A pass in the inner Great Wall. On 25 September 1937 the Eighth Route Army's 115th Division ambushed a Japanese supply column at Qiaogou, east of the pass, and won the Pingxingguan Victory, shattering the myth that “the Japanese army is invincible”.

pass:开伯尔山口.note: The gateway between Afghanistan and British India; the Third Anglo-Afghan War (May 1919) was fought along this line.

pass:忻口.note: The last barrier north of Taiyuan. In the Battle of Xinkou in October 1937, Wei Lihuang commanded the Central Army in concert with the Shanxi Army and the Eighth Route Army; army commander Hao Mengling was killed in action.

pass:惠通桥.mod: Huitong Bridge over the Nu River, on the Longling–Shidian border, Yunnan
pass:惠通桥.note: The suspension bridge carrying the Burma Road across the Nu River. On 5 May 1942 the defenders blew up the bridge, and the Japanese were held on the west bank of the Nu for two years.

pass:昆仑关.mod: Kunlun Pass, Xingning District, Nanning, Guangxi
pass:昆仑关.note: The northern screen of Nanning. In December 1939 Du Yuming's Fifth Army took Kunlun Pass, killing the Japanese brigade commander Nakamura Masao.

pass:星星峡.note: The chokepoint on the Gansu–Xinjiang border. In April 1937 more than 400 survivors of the Western Route Army arrived here and were received into Xinjiang by Chen Yun and others; it was also the gateway through which Soviet aid convoys for China entered Gansu.

pass:梅关.note: The pass on the ancient Dayu Ridge road, the route between Guangdong and Jiangxi. From 1934 Chen Yi and Xiang Ying kept up the Three-Year Guerrilla War in the South in the Youshan area beside it.

pass:武胜关.mod: Wusheng Pass, on the Xinyang (Henan)–Guangshui (Hubei) border
pass:武胜关.note: The passage of the Beijing–Hankou Railway between the Dabie and Tongbai mountains, on the Henan–Hubei boundary. The Japanese took it in October 1938, and Wuhan's northern gateway was lost.

pass:泸定桥.note: The iron-chain bridge over the Dadu River, a key crossing between Sichuan and Xikang. On 29 May 1935 the Red Army seized Luding Bridge in a swift assault, escaping the danger of repeating Shi Dakai's fate.

pass:潘绍山口.note: A pass in the Patkai Hills; the China–India Road crossed it from Ledo into Burma, and it was called “Hell's Gate”.

pass:潼关.mod: Gangkou Town, Tongguan, Shaanxi (old Tongguan town)
pass:潼关.note: The strategic crossroads of Shaanxi, Shanxi and Henan. During the War of Resistance the Japanese held Fenglingdu on the north bank of the Yellow River and shelled across the river for seven years, but never managed to cross westward into Guanzhong.

pass:畹町桥.note: The China–Burma boundary bridge carrying the Burma Road across the Wanding River. In May 1942 the Japanese entered Yunnan by it; in January 1945 the Chinese Army in India and the Chinese Expeditionary Force from western Yunnan joined up nearby at Mong Yu.

pass:腊子口.note: A gorge pass between Sichuan and Gansu. On 17 September 1935 the Red First Army Group broke through Lazikou, held by Lu Dachang's forces, and opened the way north.

pass:西里西亚门.note: The ancient route through the Taurus Mountains to the Anatolian plateau; the Baghdad Railway crossed it by tunnel, and the Taurus section was not completed until the end of the First World War.

pass:镇南关.note: A key pass on the China–Vietnam border. In September 1940 the Japanese moved into northern Vietnam along this line; in December 1949 the remnants of Huang Jie's KMT army group withdrew into Vietnam around here.

pass:雁门关.note: A key pass in the inner Great Wall and the screen of northern Shanxi. In October 1937 the Eighth Route Army's 120th Division ambushed a Japanese transport column south of Yanmen Pass.

rail:东印度—西北铁路干线.mod: now trunk lines of India and Pakistan
rail:东印度—西北铁路干线.note: From Calcutta across the Ganges plain via Delhi and Lahore to Peshawar, completed in stages in the late 19th century; the trunk line was straightened in 1906. At the Partition of India in 1947, refugees on trains through the Punjab were repeatedly massacred.
rail:东印度—西北铁路干线.old: East Indian and North Western Railway main line

rail:东海道·山阳本线.mod: now the Tokaido and Sanyo Main Lines (Japan)
rail:东海道·山阳本线.note: From Tokyo via Nagoya, Kyoto, Osaka and Kobe to Shimonoseki; the Tokaido Line was completed in 1889 and the Sanyo Line in 1901; from Shimonoseki the Kanpu ferry crossed to Busan, and in 1942 the Kanmon Tunnel opened, linking Kyushu.

rail:个碧石铁路.note: A 600-millimetre-gauge railway built by the gentry and merchants of southern Yunnan themselves to carry Gejiu tin; the Bisezhai–Gejiu section opened in November 1921, and it was extended to Jianshui in 1928 and to Shiping in 1936.

rail:中东铁路.mod: now the Harbin–Manzhouli and Harbin–Suifenhe Railways
rail:中东铁路.note: A shortcut for the Trans-Siberian Railway built by Russia on borrowed Chinese land, running east out through Suifenhe to join the Ussuri Railway. Under joint Sino-Soviet management from 1924; the Chinese Eastern Railway Incident took place in 1929; in March 1935 the Soviet Union sold it to Puppet Manchukuo in disregard of the Chinese government's protests; after August 1945, together with the Harbin–Dalian section, it became the Chinese Changchun Railway under joint Sino-Soviet management, and under the relevant agreement of the 1950 Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance, the Soviet Union handed it over to China without compensation on 31 December 1952.

rail:中东铁路南支线（哈尔滨—长春）.mod: now the Harbin–Changchun section of the Beijing–Harbin Railway
rail:中东铁路南支线（哈尔滨—长春）.note: After the Russo-Japanese War the line was divided at Kuanchengzi, the part to the north remaining Russian; in 1935 it was sold to Puppet Manchukuo along with the North Manchuria Railway and converted to standard gauge.

rail:中亚铁路.mod: now the Turkmen and Uzbek trunk lines and the Orenburg–Tashkent Railway
rail:中亚铁路.note: The Transcaspian Railway reached Tashkent in 1899, and the Orenburg–Tashkent Railway opened in January 1906, directly linking Central Asia with Russia proper. In 1918–1920 the Red Army fought the Whites and the Basmachi along the line.

rail:乌苏里铁路.mod: now the Khabarovsk–Vladivostok section of the Trans-Siberian Railway
rail:乌苏里铁路.note: From Vladivostok to Khabarovsk, opened in 1897; when the Entente Powers and Japan sent troops into Siberia in 1918–1922, they landed at Vladivostok.

rail:京元线.mod: now the Gyeongwon Line (South Korea) and the Kangwon Line (North Korea)
rail:京元线.note: From Keijo to Wonsan, opened in August 1914, crossing the middle of the Korean Peninsula; cut by the 38th parallel after 1945.

rail:京图铁路（敦化—图们）.mod: now the Dunhua–Tumen section of the Changchun–Tumen Railway
rail:京图铁路（敦化—图们）.note: After the September 18 Incident the Japanese went on to build the Dunhua–Tumen section, which opened in 1933; in August the Tumen River bridge came into use, connecting with the railways of northern Korea and giving Xinjing its shortest route to the ports on the Sea of Japan.

rail:京奉铁路（北宁铁路）.mod: now the Beijing–Shenyang section of the Beijing–Harbin Railway
rail:京奉铁路（北宁铁路）.note: Extended section by section from the Tangshan–Xugezhuang Railway, it reached Fengtian in the late Qing and was renamed the Beining Railway in 1929; the lifeline of communications between the lands inside and outside the Great Wall. In June 1928 Japan's Kwantung Army blew up Zhang Zuolin's train at Huanggutun; in 1933 the section beyond Shanhaiguan was placed under Puppet Manchukuo.

rail:京张铁路.mod: now the Beijing–Zhangjiakou section of the Beijing–Baotou Railway
rail:京张铁路.note: Built under the direction of Zhan Tianyou, the first trunk railway designed and built by the Chinese themselves; a switchback at Qinglongqiao carries it over Badaling; opened in September 1909.

rail:京汉铁路.mod: now the Beijing–Wuhan section of the Beijing–Guangzhou Railway
rail:京汉铁路.note: Built with Belgian loans and opened throughout in April 1906; repeatedly a main battlefield in the Northern Expedition, the Central Plains War and the War of Resistance. From 1938 its northern and southern sections were held separately by the Japanese, and in the Battle of Central Henan in 1944 the Japanese opened up the whole line.

rail:京绥铁路（大同—归绥）.mod: now the Datong–Hohhot section of the Beijing–Baotou Railway
rail:京绥铁路（大同—归绥）.note: It first reached Fengzhen in September 1915 and reached Guisui in May 1921; when Beijing was renamed Beiping in 1928, the Beijing–Suiyuan Railway was accordingly renamed the Beiping–Suiyuan Railway.

rail:京绥铁路（张家口—大同）.mod: now the Zhangjiakou–Datong section of the Beijing–Baotou Railway
rail:京绥铁路（张家口—大同）.note: The extension of the Beijing–Zhangjiakou line; it reached Yanggao in November 1911, work stopped because of the 1911 Revolution, and it reached Datong in January 1914.

rail:京釜·京义线.mod: now the Gyeongbu Line (South Korea), the Pyongui Line (North Korea) and others
rail:京釜·京义线.note: Korea's trunk line, built by Japan; the Gyeongbu Line opened in 1905 and the Gyeongui Line in 1906; in 1911 it joined the Andong–Fengtian Railway over the Yalu River bridge, giving through running from Busan to Fengtian; the main artery of Japan's continental policy of aggression.

rail:伊朗纵贯铁路.note: Built under Reza Shah, self-financed through special taxes on sugar and tea, from the Caspian Sea to the Persian Gulf, and opened in August 1938. When Britain and the Soviet Union sent troops into Iran in August 1941, the line became the “Persian Corridor” for US and British aid to the Soviet Union.

rail:北黑铁路.mod: dismantled in 1945; the present line was rebuilt in 1989
rail:北黑铁路.note: Built by Puppet Manchukuo to the bank of the Heilong River for military purposes against the Soviet Union, opened in December 1935; after Soviet forces occupied the area in 1945 they removed the rails and equipment.

rail:南浔铁路.mod: now the Nanchang–Jiujiang section of the Beijing–Kowloon Railway
rail:南浔铁路.note: Built by Jiangxi merchants, from Jiujiang to Niuhang, Nanchang, and opened in May 1916; in the Battle of Wuhan in 1938 the fighting around De'an and Wanjialing took place along the line.

rail:南满铁路.mod: now the Changchun–Shenyang section of the Beijing–Harbin Railway and the Shenyang–Dalian Railway
rail:南满铁路.note: Originally the southern branch of the Chinese Eastern Railway, seized by Japan after the Russo-Japanese War and run from 1906 by the South Manchuria Railway Company. On 18 September 1931 the Japanese blew up the track at Liutiaohu, north of Fengtian, and launched the September 18 Incident.

rail:印度支那纵贯铁路.note: The metre-gauge trunk line from Hà Nội to Sài Gòn, built in sections over more than thirty years; it was completed when the Tourane–Nha Trang section was linked up in October 1936. In 1941 the Japanese moved into southern Vietnam and used the line to carry troops south.

rail:台湾纵贯线.mod: now the Western Trunk Line, Taiwan
rail:台湾纵贯线.note: Built by the Government-General of Taiwan; the line from Keelung to Takow (Kaohsiung) was completed in 1908, the backbone of Taiwan's economy under Japanese occupation.

rail:吉敦铁路.mod: now the Jilin–Dunhua section of the Changchun–Tumen Railway
rail:吉敦铁路.note: Built under contract by the South Manchuria Railway and opened in October 1928; merged with the Jilin–Changchun Railway in November 1931.

rail:吉长铁路.mod: now the Changchun–Jilin section of the Changchun–Tumen Railway
rail:吉长铁路.note: Run jointly by China and Japan and opened in October 1912; it linked the provincial capital of Jilin to the South Manchuria Railway.

rail:同蒲铁路北段（原平—大同）.mod: now the Yuanping–Datong section of the Northern Tongpu Railway
rail:同蒲铁路北段（原平—大同）.note: When the Japanese reached Datong in August 1937 the line was still a few kilometres short of completion; the Japanese went on building it with conscripted labour and finished it in 1939.

rail:同蒲铁路北段（太原—原平）.mod: now the Taiyuan–Yuanping section of the Northern Tongpu Railway
rail:同蒲铁路北段（太原—原平）.note: The northern section of the Datong–Puzhou line first reached Yuanping in August 1935; during the Battle of Xinkou it was the Shanxi Army's rear supply line.

rail:同蒲铁路南段.note: Built by Yan Xishan with Shanxi-Suiyuan troops as labour, begun in 1933 as a narrow, metre-gauge line; the section from Taiyuan to Fenglingdu opened in stages in 1935–1936; from 1938 the Japanese advanced south along it; converted to standard gauge after the war.

rail:咸镜线.mod: now the Pyongra Line (North Korea) and others
rail:咸镜线.note: From Wonsan north along the east coast to Chongjin and Hoeryong, completed in September 1928; with the Jilin–Hoeryong and Tumen–Jiamusi lines it formed the northern route between Japan and “Manchuria”.

rail:四洮铁路.mod: now the Siping–Taonan section of the Pingqi Railway
rail:四洮铁路.note: Built with South Manchuria Railway loans; the Zhengjiatun–Tongliao branch opened first, in 1921, and the whole line in November 1923.

rail:图佳铁路.mod: now the Mudanjiang–Jiamusi Railway and the Tumen–Mudanjiang Railway
rail:图佳铁路.note: A railway running north–south through eastern Northeast China, built by Puppet Manchukuo for war against the Soviet Union, from Tumen via Mudanjiang and Linkou to Jiamusi; strong Kwantung Army forces were stationed along it.

rail:土西铁路.note: A project of the Soviet First Five-Year Plan; the tracks were joined in April 1930, linking Siberia and Central Asia. In the early part of the War of Resistance, Soviet aid for China was unloaded at Sary-Ozek station and carried east by truck through Xinjiang.

rail:天兰铁路.mod: now the Tianshui–Lanzhou section of the Longhai Railway
rail:天兰铁路.note: The section extending the Longhai Railway west to Lanzhou; begun in May 1950, it ran by way of Gangu, Longxi and Dingxi over the loess ridges and hills and opened on 1 October 1952, bringing the first trains to Lanzhou; the starting point of the later Lanzhou–Xinjiang, Baotou–Lanzhou and Lanzhou–Qinghai lines.

rail:孟买—马德拉斯铁路.note: The Great Indian Peninsula Railway and the Madras Railway met at Raichur, completing the Bombay–Madras link in 1871 and connecting India's two great ports on the west and east coasts.

rail:安奉铁路.note: A light military line built by the Japanese army during the Russo-Japanese War; in November 1911 it was rebuilt to standard gauge and the Yalu River railway bridge was completed, giving through running with the Gyeongui Line in Korea.

rail:宝天铁路.mod: now the Baoji–Tianshui section of the Longhai Railway
rail:宝天铁路.note: Cut through the gorges of the Wei River during the War of Resistance, with tunnels one after another and frequent landslides; it reached Tianshui (Beidaobu) at the end of 1945.

rail:巴格达铁路.mod: now trunk lines of Turkey, Syria and Iraq
rail:巴格达铁路.note: A project of Germany's “3B policy”, built in sections from 1903; the First World War and the post-war border changes left it broken, until in July 1940 the section in Iraq was linked up and the whole line from Istanbul to Baghdad was complete.

rail:平绥铁路（归绥—包头）.mod: now the Hohhot–Baotou section of the Beijing–Baotou Railway
rail:平绥铁路（归绥—包头）.note: It reached Baotou in January 1923, completing the whole Beiping–Suiyuan line, by which the furs, hides and grain of the Northwest were shipped east; the Guominjun's withdrawal west in 1926 and the Japanese advance west in 1937 both followed this line.

rail:广九铁路.mod: now the Guangzhou–Shenzhen Railway and the East Rail Line
rail:广九铁路.note: The British section opened in 1910 and the Chinese section in October 1911. In the early part of the War of Resistance it was the main route by which Hong Kong supplied the interior; it was cut after Guangzhou fell in October 1938.

rail:成渝铁路.note: First proposed by the Sichuan–Hankou Railway Company in the late Qing, it was repeatedly proposed and repeatedly halted in the Republican period. Begun in June 1950, with troops of the Southwest Military Region and labourers from central Sichuan as the main workforce, it opened throughout on 1 July 1952, the first trunk railway designed and built by the People's Republic of China itself.

rail:打通铁路.mod: now the Dahushan–Tongliao section of the Dazheng Railway
rail:打通铁路.note: A branch line built by the Beining Railway itself, reaching Tongliao in 1927; it ran parallel to the South Manchuria Railway, and Japan protested that it “violated the treaties”.

rail:拉滨铁路.note: Built by Puppet Manchukuo to bypass the Chinese Eastern Railway and opened in September 1934, it gave direct access to Harbin from the direction of Jilin and Korea.

rail:暹罗北线.note: From Bangkok to Chiang Mai through the Khun Tan Tunnel; it reached Chiang Mai in January 1922, bringing the old Lanna lands under Bangkok's control.

rail:暹罗南线.note: From Thonburi, Bangkok, south via Hat Yai to Padang Besar; joined to the Malayan railways in 1918, giving direct access to the mainland opposite Penang. In December 1941, after landing at Singora and Pattani, the Japanese advanced south along the line to attack Malaya.

rail:杭江铁路（萧山—兰溪）.mod: now the Xiaoshan–Jinhua section of the Shanghai–Kunming Railway
rail:杭江铁路（萧山—兰溪）.note: Built by Zhejiang Province itself, starting from the riverside at Xixing on the south bank of the Qiantang River; it reached Lanxi in March 1932 and was the forerunner of the Zhejiang–Jiangxi Railway.

rail:杭江铁路（金华—玉山）.mod: now the Jinhua–Yushan section of the Shanghai–Kunming Railway
rail:杭江铁路（金华—玉山）.note: Completed in November 1933 and formally opened in January 1934; Quzhou became the communications centre of western Zhejiang.

rail:正太铁路.note: A metre-gauge railway built with French loans, which gave rise to Shijiazhuang; after Niangzi Pass fell in October 1937 the Japanese pressed on along it to Taiyuan; converted to standard gauge in 1939, it bore the brunt of the Hundred Regiments Campaign.

rail:汉志铁路.mod: partly used in Jordan; abandoned in Saudi Arabia
rail:汉志铁路.note: Built by the Ottoman Empire in the name of the pilgrimage; the line from Damascus to Medina opened in September 1908. In 1916–1918 the forces of the Arab Revolt and Lawrence repeatedly sabotaged it, and the line south of Ma'an was abandoned from then on.

rail:江南铁路.mod: now the Nanjing–Wuhu Railway and the northern section of the Anhui–Jiangxi Railway
rail:江南铁路.note: Built by the privately owned Jiangnan Railway Company; the Wuhu–Sunjiabu section opened first, in November 1934, and the whole line from Zhonghua Gate, Nanjing, to Sunjiabu in May 1935; after it fell in December 1937 it was run by the Japanese.

rail:汴洛铁路.mod: now the Kaifeng–Luoyang section of the Longhai Railway
rail:汴洛铁路.note: Built with Belgian loans, completed at the end of 1909 and opened in early 1910; it met the Beijing–Hankou line at Zhengzhou, and was merged into the Longhai Railway in 1913.

rail:沈海·吉海铁路.note: The backbone of the Northeast's own railway network: the Fengtian–Hailong Railway reached Hailong in August 1928, and the Jilin–Hailong Railway linked it to Jilin in August 1929; running parallel to and competing with the South Manchuria Railway, they were the focus of the Sino-Japanese railway dispute before the September 18 Incident.

rail:沪宁铁路（京沪铁路）.mod: now the Shanghai–Nanjing section of the Beijing–Shanghai Railway
rail:沪宁铁路（京沪铁路）.note: Built with British loans and opened in 1908; after the capital was established at Nanjing in 1928 it was renamed the Nanjing–Shanghai Railway. After the Battle of Songhu in 1937 the Japanese advanced west along it to Nanjing.

rail:沪杭甬铁路（沪杭段）.mod: now the Shanghai–Hangzhou section of the Shanghai–Kunming Railway
rail:沪杭甬铁路（沪杭段）.note: Built with funds raised by the gentry and merchants of Jiangsu and Zhejiang themselves, opened in June 1909. There were also the Ningbo–Cao'e section (1914) and the Xiaoshan–Cao'e section (November 1937); the Qiantang River Bridge opened in September 1937 and was blown up by the Chinese side itself in December, and the Hangzhou–Ningbo line was still not joined up after the war.

rail:泰缅铁路.mod: the Kanchanaburi section in Thailand is still in use; the Burmese section has been dismantled
rail:泰缅铁路.note: Built by the Japanese with conscripted Allied prisoners of war and Asian labourers to supply the Burma front; its 415 kilometres were finished in one year at the cost of more than 100,000 lives, and it was called the “Death Railway”. The tracks were joined in October 1943; the Burmese section was dismantled after the war.

rail:津浦铁路.mod: now the Tianjin–Pukou section of the Beijing–Shanghai Railway
rail:津浦铁路.note: Built with German loans for the northern section and British loans for the southern; opened throughout in November 1912 after the Yellow River railway bridge at Luokou was completed; in October 1933 the Pukou–Xiaguan train ferry linked it to the Shanghai–Nanjing line. The Battle of Xuzhou and the Huaihai Campaign were both fought along this line.

rail:洮昂铁路.mod: now the Taonan–Angangxi section of the Pingqi Railway
rail:洮昂铁路.note: Built by the Fengtian Clique in cooperation with the South Manchuria Railway, completed in July 1926. In November 1931 Ma Zhanshan held off the Japanese at the Nen River railway bridge (Jiangqiao), fighting the first battle of armed resistance to Japan in the Northeast.

rail:浙赣铁路（南昌—株洲）.mod: now the Nanchang–Zhuzhou section of the Shanghai–Kunming Railway
rail:浙赣铁路（南昌—株洲）.note: In September 1937 the Nanchang–Pingxiang section linked up with the late-Qing Zhuzhou–Pingxiang Railway (1905), completing the whole line from Hangzhou to Zhuzhou; joined to the Guangzhou–Hankou line, it became the main route for the westward withdrawal from the southeast.

rail:浙赣铁路（玉山—南昌）.mod: now the Yushan–Nanchang section of the Shanghai–Kunming Railway
rail:浙赣铁路（玉山—南昌）.note: The westward extension of the Hangzhou–Jiangshan Railway; it reached Nanchang in 1936 and was renamed the Zhejiang–Jiangxi Railway. In the Battle of Zhejiang–Jiangxi in 1942 the Japanese wrecked the line and carried off large quantities of rails.

rail:淮南铁路.note: Built by the National Construction Commission to carry Huainan coal, from Tianjia'an via Hefei to Yuxikou on the Yangtze; completed in December 1935. Destroyed by the Chinese side in 1938; in 1940 the Japanese repaired the section from Jiulonggang to Yuxikou.

rail:湖南线.note: From Daejeon across the Jeolla plain to Mokpo, opened in January 1914; used mainly to carry out the rice of the Honam plain.

rail:湘桂铁路（来宾—镇南关）.mod: now the Laibin–Pingxiang section of the Hunan–Guangxi Railway
rail:湘桂铁路（来宾—镇南关）.note: Part of the roadbed was built during the War of Resistance. Work resumed in 1950, and the line ran by way of Nanning and Chongzuo to Zhennan Pass on the China–Vietnam border (renamed Munan Pass in 1953, now Youyi Pass); it opened in October 1951.

rail:湘桂铁路（柳州—来宾）.mod: now the Liuzhou–Laibin section of the Hunan–Guangxi Railway
rail:湘桂铁路（柳州—来宾）.note: Extended from Liuzhou to Laibin in 1941, the southern end of the Hunan–Guangxi Railway's operating line in the Republican period; damaged in the Hunan–Guangxi retreat of 1944 and repaired after the war.

rail:湘桂铁路（桂林—柳州）.mod: now the Guilin–Liuzhou section of the Hunan–Guangxi Railway
rail:湘桂铁路（桂林—柳州）.note: Linked up on 16 December 1939, in time to carry troops to the Battle of Kunlun Pass; extended to Laibin in 1941. In the Republican period only the section from Hengyang to Laibin was actually in operation.

rail:湘桂铁路（衡阳—桂林）.mod: now the Hengyang–Guilin section of the Hunan–Guangxi Railway
rail:湘桂铁路（衡阳—桂林）.note: Begun in September 1937 with several hundred thousand conscripted labourers, it was finished in a single year. In 1944, in the great rout of KMT forces in the Henan–Hunan–Guangxi Campaign, refugees clung to the trains to flee south, and railway staff tore up the track and blew up bridges along the way.

rail:滇越铁路.mod: now the Kunming–Hekou Railway and Vietnam's Hà Nội–Lào Cai railway
rail:滇越铁路.note: A metre-gauge railway built by France, it reached Kunming in April 1910; Yunnan's outlet to the sea and a key route for foreign aid in the early part of the War of Resistance. When the Japanese moved into northern Vietnam in September 1940, the Chinese side blew up the Hekou bridge and dismantled the Hekou–Bisezhai section.

rail:潮汕铁路.note: A merchant-run railway built with funds raised by Zhang Yunan and other overseas Chinese in Southeast Asia, opened in 1906; dismantled around the time Shantou fell in June 1939.

rail:粤汉铁路（广州—韶关）.mod: now the Guangzhou–Shaoguan section of the Beijing–Guangzhou Railway
rail:粤汉铁路（广州—韶关）.note: Built by Guangdong merchants, it reached Shaoguan in June 1916; the Northern Expedition Army went north along it into Hunan in 1926.

rail:粤汉铁路（株洲—韶关）.mod: now the Zhuzhou–Shaoguan section of the Beijing–Guangzhou Railway
rail:粤汉铁路（株洲—韶关）.note: Completed with the Boxer Indemnity funds returned by Britain, it crosses the Nanling Mountains; on 1 September 1936 the whole Guangzhou–Hankou line opened, running straight through from Guangzhou to Wuchang. From 1938 its northern and southern ends were in enemy hands, and in 1944 the Japanese Operation Ichi-gō aimed to open up this line.

rail:粤汉铁路（武昌—株洲）.mod: now the Wuchang–Zhuzhou section of the Beijing–Guangzhou Railway
rail:粤汉铁路（武昌—株洲）.note: The Changsha–Zhuzhou section opened first, in the late Qing; the section from Xujiapeng, Wuchang, to Changsha opened in September 1918. The Northern Expedition battles of Tingsiqiao and Heshengqiao and the three Battles of Changsha were all fought along the line.

rail:缅甸铁路干线.note: The railway of British Burma, which reached Mandalay in 1889 and was extended to Myitkyina around 1899, with a Mandalay–Lashio branch connecting with the Burma Road. In 1942 the Chinese Expeditionary Force fought along the line, and in August 1944 Chinese and US forces took Myitkyina.

rail:胶济铁路.note: Built by Germany and opened in June 1904. Seized by Japanese forces in October 1914 and redeemed by China in January 1923 under the Washington Conference; it fell again in December 1937.

rail:苏嘉铁路.note: A link line built for national defence to bypass Shanghai, opened in July 1936, connecting the Nanjing–Shanghai and Shanghai–Hangzhou lines; dismantled by the Japanese in 1944.

rail:西伯利亚大铁路.mod: now the western Trans-Siberian Railway and the Transbaikal Railway
rail:西伯利亚大铁路.note: From Chelyabinsk via Irkutsk and Chita to Manzhouli, joining the Chinese Eastern Railway for through running to Vladivostok; the Circum-Baikal section was linked up in 1904. In 1918–1920 it was the lifeline fought over by the Red Army against the Czechoslovak Legion and Kolchak's White Army.

rail:锦承铁路.note: Built by the Japanese and puppet authorities after Rehe fell in 1933, from Jinzhou via Chaoyang and Yebaishou to Chengde, and opened in sections in the mid-1930s; it was later extended to Gubeikou, and the Chengde–Gubeikou section was dismantled in 1945.

rail:阿穆尔铁路.mod: now the Kuenga–Khabarovsk section of the Trans-Siberian Railway
rail:阿穆尔铁路.note: Built by Russia after the Russo-Japanese War so as not to pass through Chinese territory; in October 1916 the Heilong River bridge at Khabarovsk came into use, and the Trans-Siberian Railway was complete entirely within Russia's own territory.

rail:陇海铁路（开封—徐州）.mod: now the Kaifeng–Xuzhou section of the Longhai Railway
rail:陇海铁路（开封—徐州）.note: Work began at both ends in 1913; completed in May 1915 and formally opened in January the following year, it met the Tianjin–Pukou line at Xuzhou.

rail:陇海铁路（徐州—海州）.mod: now the Xuzhou–Lianyungang section of the Longhai Railway
rail:陇海铁路（徐州—海州）.note: Built with Dutch loans, it reached Haizhou (Xinpu) in 1925, and in 1934 was extended to the new port at Laoyao, which is Lianyungang.

rail:陇海铁路（洛阳—观音堂）.mod: now the Luoyang–Sanmenxia section of the Longhai Railway
rail:陇海铁路（洛阳—观音堂）.note: Begun in 1910, it first reached Tiemen in 1912 and was extended to Guanyintang in the early Republican years; for more than ten years thereafter this was the western end of the Longhai line.

rail:陇海铁路（潼关—西安）.mod: now the Tongguan–Xi'an section of the Longhai Railway
rail:陇海铁路（潼关—西安）.note: Begun in August 1932, it reached Xi'an in December 1934, and from then on the Northwest was connected with the eastern railway network.

rail:陇海铁路（灵宝—潼关）.mod: now the Lingbao–Tongguan section of the Longhai Railway
rail:陇海铁路（灵宝—潼关）.note: Begun in November 1930, it reached Tongguan in December 1931. During the War of Resistance the section east of Tongguan was shelled by the Japanese from across the Yellow River, and trains ran through at night with their lights out; they were called “pass-running trains”.

rail:陇海铁路（西安—宝鸡）.mod: now the Xi'an–Baoji section of the Longhai Railway
rail:陇海铁路（西安—宝鸡）.note: Begun in January 1935, it reached Baoji in December 1936; during the War of Resistance it was the hub linking Guanzhong with the Sichuan–Shaanxi Highway.

rail:陇海铁路（观音堂—灵宝）.mod: now the Sanmenxia–Lingbao section of the Longhai Railway
rail:陇海铁路（观音堂—灵宝）.note: Extended with Belgian loans, it reached Lingbao in 1927.

rail:马来亚铁路西海岸线.note: From Butterworth (opposite Penang) to Johore Bahru, linked up in 1909; in 1923 the Johore Causeway opened, giving direct access to Singapore. From December 1941 to February 1942 the Japanese fought their way down this line to Singapore in a little over fifty days.

rail:黔桂铁路（柳州—金城江）.mod: now the Liuzhou–Jinchengjiang section of the Guizhou–Guangxi Railway
rail:黔桂铁路（柳州—金城江）.note: Begun in July 1939 for the needs of the War of Resistance, it reached Jinchengjiang at the end of 1940; destroyed in the fighting in the winter of 1944 and repaired in 1949.

rail:黔桂铁路（金城江—独山）.mod: now the Jinchengjiang–Dushan section of the Guizhou–Guangxi Railway
rail:黔桂铁路（金城江—独山）.note: Reached Dushan in June 1943, with track laid nearly to Duyun. In November–December 1944 the Japanese drove into southern Guizhou, Dushan fell, and the line was almost entirely wrecked.

rail:齐克铁路.mod: now the Qiqihar–Yi'an section of the Qibei Railway
rail:齐克铁路.note: Built by Heilongjiang Province itself, it reached Tai'an (now Yi'an) in January 1931; extended under Puppet Manchukuo, it reached Bei'an in November 1933.

range:中条山.note: Uplands of southern Shanxi. In 1938–1941 Chinese forces held them and tied down the Japanese for three years; they were lost in the Battle of the Zhongtiao Mountains in May 1941.

range:五台山.note: In November 1937 the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Military Region was established at Wutai, and Nie Rongzhen made this the centre of the base area.

range:六盘山.note: In October 1935 the Central Red Army crossed the Liupan Mountains, and Mao Zedong wrote the poem Qing Ping Yue: Mount Liupan; the army then reached Wuqizhen in northern Shaanxi.

range:南岭.note: The watershed between the Yangtze and Pearl river systems; the Northern Expedition setting out, the Long March breaking through the blockade lines and Operation Ichi-gō all had to cross it.

range:吕宋科迪勒拉.note: Uplands of northern Luzon; in 1945 Yamashita Tomoyuki withdrew the Japanese forces here and held out until Japan's defeat.

range:吕梁山.note: Uplands of western Shanxi, bordered by the Yellow River to the west; during the War of Resistance they shielded the 120th Division's Northwestern Shanxi (Shanxi-Suiyuan) Base Area.

range:唐努山.note: Between Tannu Uriankhai and Outer Mongolia.

range:喜马拉雅山.note: The great snowy range between Xizang and British India, Nepal and Bhutan. In 1942–1945 the Hump route flew over its eastern section.

range:外兴安岭.note: The China–Russia boundary range fixed by the Treaty of Nerchinsk in 1689; after 1858 it lay inside Russia.

range:大兴安岭.note: The western edge of the Northeast. In August 1945 the tank army of the Soviet Transbaikal Front crossed the range and drove straight down onto the Northeast plain.

range:大别山.note: Boundary mountains of Hubei, Henan and Anhui, home of the Hubei-Henan-Anhui Soviet Area; in August 1947 the Liu-Deng Army made its thousand-li leap forward into these mountains.

range:大巴山.note: The barrier between Hanzhong and Sichuan; in 1933–1935 the Red Fourth Front Army's Sichuan-Shaanxi Soviet Area was based in these mountains.

range:大雪山.note: Snowy mountains of Kham; on the Long March the Red Army crossed Jiajin Mountain, Mengbi Mountain and others on their eastern side.

range:天山.note: The divide between northern and southern Xinjiang.

range:太白山脉.note: The backbone of the eastern Korean Peninsula.

range:太行山.note: The roof of North China. From 1937 the Eighth Route Army's 129th Division built the Shanxi-Hebei-Henan Base Area here, and the headquarters of the Eighth Route Army and of the 129th Division were long based around Wuxiang, Liaoxian and Shexian.

range:小白山脉.note: Uplands of the southern Korean Peninsula.

range:岷山.note: Snowy mountains between Sichuan and Gansu. In September 1935 the Red Army broke through Lazikou and crossed the Min Mountains to go north.

range:帕米尔.note: Where China's Xinjiang, British India, Afghanistan and Russian Central Asia meet.

range:掸邦高原.mod: western edge of the Shan Plateau
range:掸邦高原.note: The plateau of eastern Burma; in 1942 the Japanese advanced north across it to Lashio.

range:欧文斯坦利山脉.note: The backbone of southeastern New Guinea; in 1942 Australian forces fought along the Kokoda Track to stop the Japanese from crossing the range to attack Port Moresby.

range:武夷山.note: Boundary mountains between Fujian and Jiangxi; the eastern screen of the Central Soviet Area.

range:武陵山.note: Uplands on the borders of Hunan, Hubei, Sichuan and Guizhou; in 1934–1935 the Red Second and Sixth Army Groups built the Hunan-Hubei-Sichuan-Guizhou Soviet Area here.

range:比劳克唐山脉.note: Boundary range between Thailand and Burma; in 1942–1943 the Japanese drove Allied prisoners of war and Asian labourers to build the Burma–Siam Railway, which crosses its northern section at the Three Pagodas Pass.

range:沂蒙山.note: Uplands of central Shandong, the centre of the Shandong Base Area during the War of Resistance; the Menglianggu Campaign of 1947 was fought among them.

range:燕山.note: The northern barrier of North China, with the Great Wall built along its crest. In 1933 the Great Wall Resistance was fought along the line of Xifengkou, Gubeikou and Lengkou.

range:狼林山脉.note: The backbone of northern Korea; in November 1950 it separated the eastern and western columns of the “UN Command” forces.

range:祁连山.note: The snowy range on the south side of the Hexi Corridor. In March 1937 the remnants of the Western Route Army were scattered in the Qilian Mountains; the survivors went west to Xingxingxia.

range:秦岭.note: The southern screen of Guanzhong. In 1935 the Red 25th Army entered the Hubei-Henan-Shaanxi border area; in 1949 the First Field Army and Hu Zongnan's forces faced each other along the routes through the Qinling.

range:罗霄山.note: Uplands on the Hunan–Jiangxi border; Jinggangshan, in their middle section, is where Mao Zedong and Zhu De founded the first rural base area after 1927.

range:若开山脉.note: The western barrier of Burma; in 1942–1945 the British and Japanese fought back and forth in Arakan.

range:萨彦岭.note: The barrier to the north of Tannu Uriankhai (Tuva).

range:邛崃山.note: In June 1935 the Central Red Army crossed Jiajin Mountain in this range and joined the Red Fourth Front Army at Dawei, Maogong.

range:那加山.note: Uplands between India and Burma; in 1942 the Fifth Army of the Chinese Expeditionary Force crossed the “Yeren Mountains” here to withdraw into India, and in 1944 the Japanese crossed the hills to attack Imphal and Kohima.

range:锡霍特山脉.note: The main range of Russia's Primorye.

range:长山山脉.note: The barrier between Vietnam and Laos.

range:长白山.note: Boundary mountains between China and Korea. In 1936–1941 the First Route Army of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army kept up guerrilla warfare here.

range:阴山（大青山）.note: Uplands of northern Suiyuan. In 1938 the Eighth Route Army's Daqingshan Detachment opened up a guerrilla zone here.

range:阿尔泰山.note: Where China, Mongolia and Russia meet.

range:雪峰山.note: The screen of western Hunan. In April–June 1945, in the Battle of Western Hunan (the Zhijiang operation), the Japanese were checked here.

range:马来亚中央山脉.note: The backbone of the Malay Peninsula.

range:高黎贡山.note: The great mountain range on the west bank of the Nu River; in the Western Yunnan counter-offensive of 1944, Chinese forces attacked up its slopes.

river:乌江.note: In January 1935 the Central Red Army forced a crossing of the Wu River and went on to occupy Zunyi.

river:乌苏里江.note: Boundary river between China and Russia (the Soviet Union).

river:伊洛瓦底江.note: The lifeline of Burma; in 1942 Japanese forces advanced north along the river, and in 1945 British forces came south down it and recovered Rangoon.

river:印度河.note: After the Partition of India in 1947 it flows through Pakistan; its upper course runs through Kashmir.

river:嘉陵江.note: In March–April 1935 the Red Fourth Front Army crossed the Jialing River westward, withdrawing from the Sichuan-Shaanxi Soviet Area.

river:图们江.note: Boundary river between China and Korea and between China and the Soviet Union; the Zhanggufeng Incident of 1938 took place on the east bank of its lower course.

river:大渡河.note: In May 1935 the Red Army forced a crossing at Anshunchang and seized Luding Bridge in a swift assault; Shi Dakai of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom had met his downfall here in 1863.

river:安加拉河.note: The outflow of Lake Baikal; Irkutsk stands on its banks, and Kolchak was executed here in 1920.

river:怒江.note: In May 1942 Japanese forces reached Huitong Bridge on the west bank of the Nu River; Chinese forces blew up the bridge to halt the enemy, and for the next two years the two sides faced each other across the river; in May 1944 the Chinese Expeditionary Force in western Yunnan forced a crossing of the Nu River and counter-attacked.

river:松花江.note: The great river of the Northeast heartland; in 1946–1947 the Northeast Democratic Allied Army crossed it southward in the “three crossings south of the Songhua”.

river:汉江.note: Also known as the Hanshui. The Battle of Suixian–Zaoyang in 1939 and the Battle of Zaoyang–Yichang in 1940 were fought on both banks of the Han.

river:汉江（朝鲜半岛）.note: Flows through Seoul; the Han River Bridge was blown up in June 1950.

river:洛东江.note: In August–September 1950 the “UN Command” forces built the “Busan Perimeter” along the Nakdong River.

river:洪泽湖.note: From 1938 to 1947, while the Yellow River flowed into the Huai, its waters passed through this lake to reach the Yangtze.

river:淮河.note: The dividing line between north and south. From 1938 the Yellow River took over the Huai's course, and the area north of the Huai became the Yellow River flooded area.

river:湄公河.note: Flows through Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Cochinchina; after the Franco-Thai War of 1941, Thailand gained the territories on the west bank of the Mekong.

river:湘江.note: In the Battle of the Xiang River at the end of November 1934, during the Long March, the Central Red Army broke through the fourth blockade line, its numbers falling sharply.

river:红河.note: Flows from Yunnan into Tonkin in Vietnam; the Yunnan–Vietnam Railway runs along the river.

river:约旦河.note: After the First Middle East War of 1948, Jordan gained the area on the west bank of the river.

river:萨尔温江.note: The lower course of the Nu River, flowing through the Shan States of Burma.

river:金沙江.note: In May 1935 the Central Red Army skilfully crossed the Jinsha River at Jiaopingdu, shaking off several hundred thousand pursuing troops; in April 1936 the Red Second and Sixth Army Groups crossed the river at Shigu.

river:钦敦江.note: The largest tributary of the Irrawaddy; in the Battle of Imphal in 1944 the Japanese crossed this river to advance west, and suffered heavy losses when they fell back.

river:长江.note: China's largest river. In 1938 the Battle of Wuhan was fought along the river; with the Yangtze River Crossing Campaign of April 1949, the Nationalist Government's plan to “divide the country along the river” came to nothing.

river:额尔古纳河.note: Boundary river between China and Russia (the Soviet Union); in the Chinese Eastern Railway Incident of 1929, Soviet forces attacked along the river.

river:鸭绿江.note: Boundary river between China and Korea. On 19 October 1950 the Chinese People's Volunteers crossed the river into Korea from Andong, Changdian Hekou and Ji'an.

river:黄河.note: In June 1938 the Nationalist Government breached the dyke at Huayuankou, Zhengzhou, to halt the enemy; the Yellow River turned southeast along the Jialu and Ying rivers, took over the course of the Huai and flowed via Hongze Lake and the Grand Canal into the Yangtze, creating the Yellow River flooded area, until the breach was closed in March 1947 and the river returned to its old course.

river:黄泛区（黄河改道）.note: On 9 June 1938 the Nationalist Government breached the southern dyke of the Yellow River at Huayuankou, Zhengzhou, using water in place of troops to hold up the Japanese advance west. The floodwaters passed Zhongmu and Weishi and flowed south along the Jialu and Ying rivers, took over the course of the Huai into Hongze Lake, and then reached the Yangtze by way of the Grand Canal; 44 counties in Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu were affected and more than 800,000 people died. In March 1947 the breach was closed and the Yellow River returned to its old course.

river:黑龙江.note: Boundary river between China and Russia (the Soviet Union).

road:中印公路（史迪威公路）.mod: now the road from Ledo, India, to Myitkyina and Bhamo, Myanmar, and G320
road:中印公路（史迪威公路）.note: Built section by section from Ledo by Chinese and US engineers following the counter-offensive of the Chinese Army in India, crossing the Yeren Mountains; on 27 January 1945 the Chinese Army in India and the Chinese Expeditionary Force from western Yunnan joined up at Mong Yu, near Wanding, and the first convoy reached Kunming on 4 February; the China–India oil pipeline ran alongside.

road:川滇西路.mod: now the Leshan–Xichang road and the Xichang–Xiangyun road
road:川滇西路.note: From Leshan via Xichang to Xiangyun, where it joined the Burma Road, bypassing Guizhou and leading straight to western Sichuan; built during the War of Resistance by several hundred thousand Yi and Han labourers, it opened in sections around 1941.

road:康藏公路.mod: the line Ya'an–Kangding–Garze–Qamdo–Lhasa, roughly today's G318 and G317
road:康藏公路.note: Begun from Ya'an in April 1950; the 18th Army and labourers from Sichuan and Xizang built the road as they advanced, crossing Erlang Mountain and Chola Mountain, then turning south at Qamdo via Bamda, Bomi and Nyingchi; it opened to Lhasa on 25 December 1954, the same day as the Qinghai–Xizang Highway, with a total length of more than 2,200 kilometres.

road:滇缅公路.mod: now G320 (Kunming–Ruili) and the Muse–Lashio road in Myanmar
road:滇缅公路.note: Yunnan conscripted 200,000 labourers to build it in a rush in nine months; opened in December 1938, it connected via Lashio with the Burmese railway to Rangoon, and after the Yunnan–Vietnam line was cut it was the only overland route for foreign aid; Britain closed it from July to October 1940. In May 1942 the Japanese took Wanding, and Huitong Bridge was blown up.

road:西北国际交通线.mod: roughly the Xinjiang and Gansu sections of the Lianyungang–Khorgas Expressway
road:西北国际交通线.note: Soviet munitions for China were unloaded at Sary-Ozek station on the Turkestan–Siberia Railway and carried by truck via Horgos, Dihua, Hami and Xingxingxia to Lanzhou, while aircraft were ferried along the route. After the Soviet–Japanese Neutrality Pact of April 1941 and the outbreak of the Soviet–German war in June, the aid basically stopped.

road:青藏公路.note: Before this, Mu Shengzhong led the Xizang Transport Corps' camel caravans by way of Xiangride and Heihe (Nagqu) to keep Lhasa supplied, with heavy losses of men and animals. In May 1954 construction began southward from Golmud; in a little over seven months the road crossed the Kunlun and Tanggula mountains, and it opened to Lhasa on 25 December.

route:“联合国军”“撕裂者作战”.note: Ridgway, with the US IX and X Corps as his main force, pushed north from the Wonju–Hoengseong line, aiming to wear down his opponent rather than to fight for towns: he occupied Hongcheon on 15 March, entered Chuncheon, already evacuated by the Chinese and Korean forces, on the 21st, and by the end of the month had pushed to near the 38th parallel. On the western front Chinese and Korean forces withdrew from Seoul on their own initiative; the US I Corps reoccupied it on the 14th–15th and made an airborne landing at Munsan on the 23rd.

route:“联合国军”东线北进.mod: Yangyang, South Korea – Hyesan, North Korea
route:“联合国军”东线北进.note: The ROK I Corps crossed the 38th parallel along the east coast on 1 October, occupying Wonsan on the 10th and Hamhung on the 17th; the US 7th Division landed at Iwon and went north via Pukchong and Pungsan, reaching Hyesan on the Yalu on 21 November.
route:“联合国军”东线北进.old: “UN Command” advance north on the eastern front

route:“联合国军”仁川登陆与北进.mod: Incheon, South Korea – Chosan, North Korea
route:“联合国军”仁川登陆与北进.note: On 15 September the US X Corps landed at Incheon, cutting the People's Army's line of retreat, and retook Seoul on the 28th; in early October the “UN Command” forces crossed the 38th parallel and advanced north, carrying the flames of war to the banks of the Yalu River; they occupied Pyongyang on the 19th, and part of the ROK 6th Division reached Chosan on the Yalu on the 26th, but was soon struck by the Chinese People's Volunteers.
route:“联合国军”仁川登陆与北进.old: “UN Command” Incheon landing and advance north

route:一号作战·湘桂.note: The Japanese 11th Army drove south on 27 May, and Changsha fell on 18 June; Fang Xianjue's Tenth Army held Hengyang for forty-seven days until the city fell on 8 August. In September the Japanese entered Guangxi; Guilin and Liuzhou fell one after the other on 10–11 November, and the vanguard advanced north along the Guizhou–Guangxi Railway, reaching Dushan on 2 December before soon pulling back; Chongqing was shaken.

route:一号作战·西江.note: The Japanese 23rd Army advanced west from Guangdong along the Xi River, occupying Wuzhou on 22 September, and via Guiping and Guixian occupied Nanning on 24 November; in December it met Japanese forces coming north from Vietnam at the border, opening the so-called continental communications line.

route:一号作战·豫中.note: The first phase of Operation Ichi-gō. The Japanese North China Area Army crossed the Yellow River at Zhongmu on 18 April, occupied Zhengzhou on the 20th and Xuchang on 1 May, then advanced west with a tank division; Luoyang fell on the 25th. Tang Enbo's forces were routed, and more than thirty counties of central Henan fell.

route:一野第一兵团进军青海.note: After the Fu-Mei Campaign, Wang Zhen's 1st Army Group advanced west from Baoji via Tianshui, Longxi and Lintao to take Linxia, crossed the Yellow River northward and liberated Xining on 5 September; Ma Bufang had fled after his defeat at Lanzhou.
route:一野第一兵团进军青海.old: First Field Army's 1st Army Group advances into Qinghai

route:一野进军兰州.note: The First Field Army liberated Xi'an on 20 May, defeated Hu Zongnan's forces in the Fu-Mei Campaign in July, then advanced west into eastern Gansu along the Xi'an–Lanzhou Highway via Pingliang and Dingxi, and liberated Lanzhou on 26 August, wiping out Ma Bufang's main force.
route:一野进军兰州.old: First Field Army advances on Lanzhou

route:一野进军河西与新疆.note: After the Lanzhou Campaign the First Field Army advanced west along the Hexi Corridor, liberating Wuwei on 16 September; on the 25th the Jiuquan garrison announced an uprising by circular telegram; on the same day Tao Zhiyue in Xinjiang, and on the next day Burhan, announced uprisings by circular telegram, and Xinjiang was peacefully liberated. The 1st Army Group went out through Xingxingxia into Xinjiang, and its vanguard entered Dihua on 20 October.
route:一野进军河西与新疆.old: First Field Army advances into the Hexi Corridor and Xinjiang

route:三野第三十五军解放南京.note: After the Yangtze River Crossing Campaign began, the KMT defenders of Nanjing and the organs of the Nationalist Government left the city on 22 April; on the 23rd the Third Field Army's 35th Army crossed the river from Pukou into Nanjing, and Nanjing was liberated; on the 24th it occupied the Presidential Palace, proclaiming the downfall of KMT rule on the mainland.
route:三野第三十五军解放南京.old: Third Field Army's 35th Army liberates Nanjing

route:三野进军福建.note: Ye Fei's 10th Army Group of the Third Field Army went south from southern Jiangsu in July, crossed the Xianxia Mountains into Fujian, and liberated Fuzhou on 17 August, Zhangzhou on 19 September and Xiamen on 17 October; its attack on Kinmen on the 25th failed.
route:三野进军福建.old: Third Field Army advances into Fujian

route:东北野战军入关.note: After the Liaoshen Campaign ended, the main force of the Northeast Field Army, about 800,000 strong, secretly moved into North China ahead of schedule in late November, by separate routes through Xifengkou and Lengkou in eastern Hebei and through Shanhaiguan, and together with the North China forces encircled Beiping and Tianjin; Tianjin was liberated on 15 January 1949, Fu Zuoyi accepted peaceful reorganization, and Beiping was peacefully liberated on the 31st.
route:东北野战军入关.old: Northeast Field Army enters North China

route:东路军入闽.note: He Yingqin's Eastern Route Army, left behind to hold the Chaozhou–Meizhou area, defeated Zhou Yinren's Fujian Army, which had invaded Guangdong, at Songkou and Yongding in October, then counter-attacked into Fujian, advancing north via Zhangzhou and Quanzhou and entering Fuzhou in December; Fujian came over to the Nationalist Government, and the Eastern Route Army turned into Zhejiang from northern Fujian and eastern Jiangxi.

route:东路军进取沪杭.note: Bai Chongxi, front-line commander-in-chief of the Eastern Route Army, entered Zhejiang from eastern Jiangxi; Zhou Fengqi of the Zhejiang Army changed sides; in February Bai defeated Sun Chuanfang's forces at Tonglu and entered Hangzhou on the 18th, and in March he advanced north along the Shanghai–Hangzhou Railway; on the 21st the CPC-led Third Armed Uprising of the Shanghai Workers took Shanghai, and on the 22nd the Eastern Route Army entered Shanghai. On the 24th Cheng Qian's forces of the Right Bank Army entered Nanjing.
route:东路军进取沪杭.old: Eastern Route Army advances on Shanghai and Hangzhou

route:中原突围.note: KMT forces 300,000 strong encircled the Central Plains Liberated Area and launched a massive attack on 26 June, and full-scale civil war broke out. Li Xiannian, Wang Zhen and others led the main force of the northern route west from Xuanhuadian, crossed the Beiping–Hankou Railway on the night of the 29th, passed through the Tongbai Mountains, crossed the Tang and Bai rivers, and reached the Henan–Hubei–Shaanxi border in mid-July, entering southern Shaanxi; Pi Dingjun's brigade went east to Jiangsu and Anhui, and Wang Zhen's forces later returned north to the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region.

route:中国人民志愿军入朝（东线）.note: Song Shilun's 9th Army Group entered Korea from Ji'an and Linjiang in early November, moving covertly onto the Kaema Plateau in temperatures of minus 30 °C; on the 27th it surrounded and attacked the US 1st Marine Division at Yudam-ri and Hagaru-ri by Changjin Lake, suffering very heavy losses from frostbite; the US forces broke out southward and evacuated from Hungnam on 24 December, and northeastern Korea was recovered.
route:中国人民志愿军入朝（东线）.old: Chinese People's Volunteers enter Korea (eastern front)

route:中国人民志愿军入朝（西线）.note: At dusk on 19 October Peng Dehuai led the Chinese People's Volunteers' 13th Army Group secretly across the Yalu River from Andong, Changdian Hekou and Ji'an, to resist US aggression and aid Korea, protect their homes and defend their country. On the 25th the First Campaign opened at Ryangsu-dong and Onjong, and in early November the US 1st Cavalry Division was defeated at Unsan; the Second Campaign was launched on the Chongchon River on 25 November, the “UN Command” forces on the Tokchon–Kunu-ri line were routed, and on 6 December Chinese and Korean forces recovered Pyongyang.
route:中国人民志愿军入朝（西线）.old: Chinese People's Volunteers enter Korea (western front)

route:中国远征军入缅.note: To protect the Yunnan–Burma international communications line and, at Britain's request, to help Burma resist Japan, the Fifth, Sixth and 66th Armies formed the Chinese Expeditionary Force and entered Burma. Dai Anlan's 200th Division went south by the Burma Road and by train from Lashio, arriving at Toungoo on 8 March to take over the defence; from the 19th it fought the Japanese 55th Division for twelve days before breaking out and withdrawing north.

route:中国驻印军反攻缅北.note: Sun Liren's New 38th Division and Liao Yaoxiang's New 22nd Division (expanded into the New First and New Sixth Armies from August 1944), with US equipment, struck out from Ledo, advancing as the China–India Road was being built; in March 1944 they took Maingkwan and Walawbum, in June Kamaing and Mogaung, and on 3 August, together with US forces, they took Myitkyina; they took Bhamo in December, and on 27 January 1945 joined up with the Chinese Expeditionary Force from western Yunnan at Mong Yu, and the China–India Road opened.
route:中国驻印军反攻缅北.old: Chinese Army in India counter-offensive in northern Burma

route:中央红军长征.note: After the failure of the Fifth counter-“encirclement” campaign, about 86,000 men of the Central Red Army were forced to make a strategic shift. Setting out from Ruijin and Yudu, they broke through four blockade lines, losing more than half their strength in the Battle of the Xiang River; at Tongdao they changed direction into Guizhou, and the Zunyi Meeting established Mao Zedong's leading position in the Party Central Committee and the Red Army; crossing the Chishui River four times, they shook off their pursuers, then skilfully crossed the Jinsha River, forced a crossing of the Dadu River and crossed Jiajin Mountain to join the Red Fourth Front Army at Maogong; holding to the policy of going north to resist Japan, they crossed the grasslands, broke through Lazikou and reached Wuqizhen on 19 October 1935, about 7,000 strong.
route:中央红军长征.old: Long March of the Central Red Army

p.二郎滩（四渡赤水）: Erlangtan (fourth crossing of the Chishui River)
p.土城（一渡赤水）: Tucheng (first crossing of the Chishui River)
p.太平渡（二渡赤水）: Taipingdu (second crossing of the Chishui River)
p.茅台（三渡赤水）: Maotai (third crossing of the Chishui River)

route:二次北伐·晋军入京.note: Yan Xishan's Third Army Group came out through Niangzi Pass and advanced north along the Beijing–Hankou Railway, facing the Fengtian Army in a stand-off around Baoding; on 4 June Zhang Zuolin, heading back beyond the Great Wall, was killed at Huanggutun by a Japanese bomb. On the 8th the Shanxi Army entered Beijing, which was renamed Beiping, and the Northern Expedition was complete.
route:二次北伐·晋军入京.old: Second Northern Expedition: Shanxi Army enters Beijing

route:二次北伐·津浦路.note: In April 1928 Chiang Kai-shek's First Army Group advanced north along the Tianjin–Pukou Railway and entered Jinan on 1 May; the Japanese, on the pretext of protecting their nationals, perpetrated the Jinan Massacre, and the Northern Expedition Army detoured across the Yellow River to continue its advance, moving forward alongside Feng Yuxiang's Second Army Group between the Beijing–Hankou and Tianjin–Pukou lines; in June the Fengtian Army withdrew beyond the Great Wall, and Tianjin changed hands.

route:二野第三兵团进军川东与成都.note: Chen Xilian's 3rd Army Group and part of the Fourth Field Army entered eastern Sichuan from western Hubei and western Hunan on 1 November, advanced north via Qianjiang, Pengshui and Nanchuan, and liberated Chongqing on the 30th; in December they pushed west on Chengdu, working with the 18th Army Group coming south from northern Sichuan to encircle and wipe out Hu Zongnan's forces; Liu Wenhui, Deng Xihou and others announced uprisings by circular telegram, and Chengdu was liberated on the 27th.
route:二野第三兵团进军川东与成都.old: Second Field Army's 3rd Army Group advances into eastern Sichuan and on Chengdu

route:二野第五兵团进军贵州.note: The Second Field Army made a wide envelopment to cut off the KMT forces' retreat into Yunnan: Yang Yong's 5th Army Group advanced west from western Hunan in early November, entering Guizhou via Zhijiang and Zhenyuan, liberated Guiyang on the 15th, and then divided its forces to push into northwestern Guizhou and southern Sichuan.
route:二野第五兵团进军贵州.old: Second Field Army's 5th Army Group advances into Guizhou

route:刘邓大军挺进大别山.note: Liu Bocheng and Deng Xiaoping led the main force of the Shanxi-Hebei-Shandong-Henan Field Army, 120,000 strong, south from southwestern Shandong on 7 August, crossed the Longhai Railway, waded through the Yellow River flooded area, crossed the Sha and Ru rivers, and around the 27th crossed the Huai River into the Dabie Mountains; with no rear base, in a thousand-li leap forward, they pushed the front line from the Yellow River to the north bank of the Yangtze, raising the curtain on the strategic offensive of the People's Liberation Army.
route:刘邓大军挺进大别山.old: Liu-Deng Army thrusts into the Dabie Mountains

route:北伐军两湖战场.note: Driven forward by KMT–CPC cooperation, the National Revolutionary Army took its oath at Guangzhou on 9 July and launched the Northern Expedition; Ye Ting's Independent Regiment, with Communists as its backbone, had already entered Hunan as the vanguard in May. Tang Shengzhi's Eighth Army entered Changsha on 11 July; the Fourth and Seventh Armies broke the Miluo River defence line on 19 August, took Tingsiqiao on the 27th and routed Wu Peifu's main force at Heshengqiao on the 30th; Wuchang was besieged in early September, and on 10 October the garrison opened the gates and surrendered.

route:北伐军江西战场.note: After success in Hunan and Hubei, Chiang Kai-shek personally led the First, Second, Third and Sixth Armies into Jiangxi against Sun Chuanfang. On 19 September Cheng Qian's Sixth Army broke into Nanchang but was soon driven out; a second attack in October also failed. In early November the Seventh Army took Jiujiang, the armies closed in, and Nanchang was occupied on 8 November; Sun Chuanfang's main force was destroyed in Jiangxi, and the Nationalist Government then moved north to Wuhan.

route:南昌起义军南下.note: On 1 August Zhou Enlai, He Long, Ye Ting, Zhu De, Liu Bocheng and others led the Nanchang Uprising, firing the first shot of armed resistance against the KMT reactionaries; from the 3rd the forces marched south, entering southern Jiangxi via Linchuan and Guangchang; after the Battle of Huichang they turned into western Fujian and went down the Ting River; in late September they took Chaozhou and Shantou, with Zhu De holding Sanheba. The main force suffered a setback at Tangkeng and was scattered at Liusha, Puning, in early October; the survivors went separately to Hailufeng and southern Hunan.

route:四野南下两湖、广西.mod: Hankou, Hubei – Youyi Pass, Pingxiang, Guangxi
route:四野南下两湖、广西.note: The Fourth Field Army liberated Wuhan on 16–17 May; in August Cheng Qian and Chen Mingren announced an uprising at Changsha by circular telegram, and Hunan was peacefully liberated; in September–October the army defeated Bai Chongxi's main force in the Hengyang–Baoqing Campaign, entered Guangxi in November, liberated Guilin on the 22nd and Nanning on 4 December, and reached Zhennan Pass on the 11th; most of Bai Chongxi's forces were wiped out or withdrew into Vietnam and to Hainan.
route:四野南下两湖、广西.old: Fourth Field Army drives south through Hubei, Hunan and Guangxi

route:国民军联军五原誓师东出.note: Feng Yuxiang returned from the Soviet Union and took the oath at Wuyuan on 17 September 1926, becoming commander-in-chief of the Guominjun Allied Army, and the whole army joined the KMT. Passing through Ningxia and Pingliang into Shaanxi, the allied army lifted the eight-month siege of Xi'an on 28 November; in May 1927 it advanced east out through Tongguan, occupying Luoyang on the 28th and entering Zhengzhou in June, where it joined the Northern Expedition Army from Wuhan in Henan.
route:国民军联军五原誓师东出.old: Guominjun Allied Army marches east after the Wuyuan oath
